**Summary Of Contributions:**
- The authors present a new method for error detection in integrated circuits image segmentation via graph neural networks. 
- This is supported by a theoretical framework for the study of IC segmentation masks as well as experiments.
- This is an industry-related application, somewhat niche, but quite interesting and relevant. The method seems to be well thought out and explicitly tailored to this application.
- The study results demonstrate that the method produces good results.

- The method presented is based on image segmentation. There is no analysis of how different segmentation methods affect the performance of the method presented. 
- I am missing a related work section that specifically addresses similar work (graph-based approaches) and other image analysis methods. The baselines seems outdated. 
- The authors argue that precise segmentation of IC structures is important for failure analysis, which, as I understand it, refers to chip defects. However, the method deals exclusively with segmentation errors. A segmentation error can look like a chip defect, or a real defect can be overlooked due to poor segmentation. The distinction between these two types of errors is not highlighted.

**Claims Explanation:**
Some claims are made, but in my opinion they are not really proven, e.g.: 
- "Moreover, segmentation errors, such as short and open circuits, can have subtle visual manifestations that are challenging to detect using conventional image analysis techniques" - This was not explained further, but only older sources were cited, and only two baselines were used in the experiments.
- "segmentation errors in IC images are typically local in nature (cf. Fig. 1), while holistic approaches offer limited explainability regarding which specific circuit elements are erroneous." - On the one hand, I find that the concept of explainability is only vaguely explained at the beginning, as it is a question of pointing out specific components that have errors and not just pure binary classification at image level. On the other hand, limited explainability is mentioned in relation to other methods, but there is no explanation of what this looks like. 
- "As we have highlighted in Section 1, unlike natural images, the correctness of structural topology is a more important aspect for the functionality of an IC." - I don't think this was emphasized in the introduction, nor do the experiments show this, since CV and anomaly detection models partly perform better than the graph-based method.

**Audience Explanation:**
The authors present a different approach to error detection in IC image segmentation that yields good results, so the work could be of interest to certain scientific fields. However, the work seems a little outdated, as no references from the last two years are cited.

**Requested Changes:**
Critical changes:
- I find the abstract very concise and difficult to understand. In addition, several abbreviations are used without being introduced. 
- Conventional image analysis techniques are mentioned, but not explained in detail. 
- Wikipedia should not be used as a reference. 
- Figure 1 is intended to highlight segmentation errors, so these should also be visually emphasized.
- "For the high-level idea, we encode each..." - The notation belongs in the method or preliminaries, but not really in the introduction - here, high-level explanations and, in particular, motivation should be provided. 
- I don't think section 2 is integrated in a meaningful way. Section 2.1 consists only of a very short section, which could be included in the method. And section 2.2 is illogical in terms of order, as GNNs are introduced briefly at the beginning, but are the last step in the pipeline.
- "the following features of component graphs are potentially useful for classification:" - Only potentially? It is only briefly mentioned, but not further explained or elaborated on. 
- The datasets should be described in more detail, especially with regard to the differences between them (apart from the number of images). Are they proprietary datasets or freely available? 
- A related work section is missing. 
- "We evaluate its performance on error detection by comparing it with several similarly constructed GNN-based detection models." - The methodological differences should be highlighted. 
- The citations are inaccurate, often only abbreviations of the conference are used. In addition, for example, the “Graph attention networks” paper was accepted at ICLR 2018.


Minor:
- "Error Detection in (given) IC image segmentation." - Only one bullet point looks out of place; I would adjust the layout.
- "and M is the ground-truth mask M"

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
NA

**Additional Comments:**
Questions:
- The image-to-graph conversion is very hand-crafted. Why was this approach chosen and not, for example, a keypoint/skeleton neural network trained on this data? 
- "It is passed through an MLP to generate two probability weights for the classes." - It is a binary classification, so one output value is sufficient. Why are two probabilities needed? 
- How are the (predicted) binary segmentation masks obtained? 
- The class imbalance is very large. Is the use of weighted cross-entropy loss sufficient? 
- Was the architecture of the EA-GIN obtained through ablation, or why this number of layers/neurons?
- Is this the first method that works also at the object level and not just at the image level?

**Summary Of Contributions:**
This paper addresses the problem of error detection in integrated circuit (IC) image segmentation, focusing on identifying local topological errors such as open circuits, short circuits, noise artifacts, and holes in segmentation masks. Unlike prior CNN-based approaches that operate holistically at the image level, the authors propose an explainable, graph-based framework that converts each connected component of a segmentation mask into a feature-annotated graph. The approach is evaluated on four IC datasets with varying complexity. Results show strong performance, especially in cross-dataset generalization, and the model demonstrates the ability to localize error-causing components, supporting its explainability claims.

Key Strengths:
 
1.) Reframing IC segmentation error detection as a graph classification problem is well motivated and technically sound. The component-level graph representation naturally supports error localization, which is valuable for hardware assurance workflows.

2.) The ability to pinpoint which specific component is erroneous, moving beyond a binary image-level error flag. This is crucial for practical debugging and hardware assurance.

3.) EA-GIN consistently outperforms baseline GNNs and compares favorably with CNN-based detectors, particularly in cross-dataset generalization, a critical requirement for industrial deployment where training data may be limited or varied.

4.) The skeleton-based graph extraction and the use of both node and edge features are carefully justified.

5.) The inclusion of a theoretical appendix (Appendix A) formalizing errors (open/short circuits, noise, holes) using metric and topological concepts supports the intuition behind the method.


Key Weaknesses:

1.) The authors should have discussed computational overhead. Like, the pipeline involves skeletonization, graph construction, and per-component GNN inference. A discussion of the runtime or computational cost compared to an end-to-end CNN would be useful for assessing practical deployment trade-offs.

2.) The method assumes reasonably accurate segmentation masks; failure modes under poor segmentation are not fully explored. Also, the contribution of individual node and edge features is not systematically evaluated.

3.) The graph conversion relies heavily on the quality of the morphological skeletonization step. The paper briefly mentions artifacts (Remark 1) but does not deeply analyze failure cases or robustness limits when skeletons are noisy or incorrectly extracted.

4.) The method is primarily validated on detecting topological anomalies (shorts/opens) and noise. Its effectiveness on other semantic error types (e.g., minor width variations, material misclassifications) is less clear.

5.) While justified, the node and edge features are hand-crafted. An ablation study or discussion on the necessity and contribution of each feature type would strengthen the methodology section.

6.) The description of edge feature construction (Equation 2, Fig. 5) could be slightly clearer. Specifically, how the perpendicular width is calculated from the binary mask (not the skeleton) at the k sample points could be elaborated.

7.) In Section 4.3, the intriguing result that training on smaller datasets (A1/A2) sometimes generalizes better to S2 than training on S2 itself is noted but not deeply analyzed. A brief hypothesis on why this occurs (e.g., overfitting on larger, noisier datasets; limited topological vocabulary) would enhance the discussion.

**Claims Explanation:**
The paper's main claims-: improved error detection accuracy, strong generalization, and enhanced explainability are largely supported by empirical evidence:

1.) The experimental design is substantial. The use of four distinct datasets (A1, A2, S1, S2) with varying complexity demonstrates robustness. Quantitative results (Tables 2 & 3) show EA-GIN's superior F1-scores against strong baselines (GIN, GINE, EGAT, CensNet, ED-ResNet, OCGTI). The cross-dataset generalization tests are particularly compelling evidence of the method's strength and practicality. Qualitative results (Figs. 6 & 7) effectively visualize the explainability claim, showing precise error localization.

2.) The methodology is explained step-by-step, from high-level motivation (Section 3.1) to detailed graph construction (Section 3.2) and model architecture (Section 3.3). Figures 3, 4, and 5 are helpful in visualizing the pipeline.

3.) The localization capability is demonstrated through component-level detection results and visual examples (Figures 6 and 7), which align well with the explainability claims.

**Audience Explanation:**
Yes, the paper is clearly relevant to TMLR's audience and broader ML community. 

1.) It presents a novel application of GNNs (with a tailored architecture, EA-GIN) to a structured, non-social, industrial domain. The focus on edge features and explainability is relevant to ongoing GNN research.

2.) The work provides a concrete case study in inherently explainable model design for a critical task, moving beyond post-hoc explanations. This is a valuable contribution to the XAI literature.

3.) It addresses a real, economically significant problem in semiconductor manufacturing and hardware assurance. Demonstrating robust cross-dataset performance is key for industrial relevance.

4.) The framing of the problem as graph-level classification or outlier detection connects to active research in anomaly detection on non-Euclidean data.

5.) The findings offer both a practical solution to an important problem and methodological insights (graph representation, edge-feature integration, explainable design) that can inspire researchers in related fields (e.g., circuit verification, biomedical image analysis).

**Requested Changes:**
1.) The paper should include an ablation analysis isolating:
    a) Node features vs edge features
    b) Width statistics vs geometric features
    c) Positional features vs purely topological features

This is essential to validate the design choices and confirm that performance gains are not incidental.

2.) The authors should have reported the average graph construction time per image, inference time per graph/image, and memory footprint trends with increasing component count. This is critical for assessing industrial applicability.

3.) The paper should explicitly discuss scenarios where the method may fail, such as severe over-segmentation or under-segmentation, skeletonization errors in noisy masks, and components with ambiguous topology.

4.) Metrics such as top-k localization accuracy (beyond F1) or component-level precision/recall would strengthen the explainability claims.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
The work has primarily positive implications for improving the efficiency, accuracy, and automation of hardware assurance in the semiconductor industry, which is critical for technological advancement and supply chain security. Potential broader impacts include:

1.) While the paper focuses on error detection for quality assurance, similar techniques for analyzing IC layouts could potentially be repurposed for reverse engineering or identifying hardware vulnerabilities (e.g., Trojans). This is a common concern in hardware security research.

2.) As an automation tool, it could reduce the need for manual visual inspection by experts. However, this is a standard effect of industrial automation and is likely to be offset by creating new roles in ML system maintenance and data analysis.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper proposes an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (EA-GIN) for error detection in IC image segmentation. The approach is well motivated for this specific application, where the types of segmentation errors are relatively constrained. Experiments are conducted on four proprietary datasets (A1, A2, S1, and S2). While the method shows strong performance within datasets, its reliance on supervised error labels and segmentation masks raises concerns about generalization and its positioning relative to anomaly detection literature.

**Claims Explanation:**
1. Table 4 demonstrates that the proposed approach provides explainable predictions by localizing erroneous components.

2. Tables 1 and 2 show that GINs achieve high accuracy for in-domain error detection in IC images.

3. The structured connectivity of IC layouts and dataset characteristics make GINs a suitable modeling choice for this task.

**Audience Explanation:**
1.  The use of Graph Isomorphism Networks for modeling IC topology is well motivated and appropriate for segmentation error detection.
    
2.  The overall approach is simple, and clear. But, the paper could still be improved with some additional details. 
    
3.  Incorporating edge features into GIN is novel and empirically effective.
    
4.  The method demonstrates strong within-dataset performance.

**Requested Changes:**
1. The method relies on labeled erroneous and normal regions and is trained using weighted binary cross-entropy. This deviates from standard anomaly detection assumptions, where anomalies are rare, random, and typically unlabeled. Although the paper argues that error types are limited in this domain, the supervised formulation restricts the method’s applicability to known and recurring error patterns. (which might have be the case for S1/S2)
    
2. While cross-dataset experiments are included, performance drops noticeably when transferring models trained on A1/A2 to S1/S2. This suggests that component structures or error distributions differ across datasets. A deeper analysis is needed to clarify whether these datasets share common topological patterns and to explain the observed performance degradation.
    
3. The paper does not sufficiently discuss or compare how the proposed method relates to unsupervised or reconstruction-based anomaly detection approaches, which are common. Why it is not useful to train them? Despite this, the method ultimately trains a supervised classifier, creating a mismatch between framing and methodology.
    
4.   The paper lacks a clear description of the four datasets (A1, A2, S1, S2). Since the datasets appear to be private and the codebase is not publicly available, reproducibility and broader applicability of the method are limited.
    
5. The paper states that weighted cross-entropy is used to address class imbalance, but does not explain how the class weights are computed. This information is important for reproducibility and fair comparison.
    
6. The paper claims that EA-GIN is complementary to CV-based approaches such as ED-ResNet. However, no hybrid or joint model is evaluated, and no improvement in end-to-end detection performance is demonstrated. As a result, this claim remains largely speculative.
    
7. In the explainability study, Top-K components are evaluated only for images where ED-ResNet successfully detects errors. Consequently, all cases missed by ED-ResNet are excluded from the EA-GIN evaluation, preventing an assessment of whether EA-GIN can recover detection failures of the CV model. The explainability claim is therefore limited to post-hoc localization rather than improving detection robustness.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
There are no broader impact concerns associated with this work.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
This submission studies bi-criteria combinatorial optimization when function evaluations are noisy, and connects offline bi-criteria approximation to online learning with bandit feedback via a new stability notion (“resilience”).

- **A bi-criteria resilience definition.** The paper introduces **(α, β, δ, N)-resilience** for bi-criteria approximation algorithms, intended to quantify how _both_ the objective approximation and constraint satisfaction degrade under bounded (potentially adversarial) oracle perturbations, while tracking the number of oracle calls **N** and the noise-sensitivity **δ**.
    
- **A black-box offline-to-online reduction for bi-criteria CMAB with bandit feedback.** Given an offline algorithm with such resilience, the paper provides a generic **explore-then-exploit** conversion that estimates queried action values via repeated bandit plays and feeds empirical means as approximate oracles to the offline routine.
    
- **General regret and cumulative constraint violation bounds.** The resulting online algorithm achieves **sublinear α-regret** and **sublinear cumulative constraint violation (CCV)** with rate on the order of  
    
    $\tilde{O}\left(\delta^{2/3}hN^{1/3}T^{2/3}\right)$
     
    (up to log factors), without assuming linearity/submodularity/semi-bandit feedback on the _noisy_ functions.
    
- **Resilience proofs for several canonical greedy bi-criteria algorithms.** The paper establishes resilience (with explicit parameters) for greedy algorithms in **Submodular Cover (SC)**, **Submodular Cost Submodular Cover (SCSC)**, and **Fair Submodular Maximization (FSM)**, including handling the technical issue that noise can destroy submodularity/monotonicity of the observed oracle.
    
- **A diagnostic/correction regarding prior resilience claims.** It provides a counterexample to a claimed extension in prior work (as stated in the paper), highlighting subtlety in generalizing greedy density arguments under inexact oracles.



Key strengths:

- **Clean abstraction** (bi-criteria resilience) that is well-matched to an offline-to-online reduction.
- **General reduction** that does not rely on semi-bandit feedback or special reward structure (beyond boundedness + concentration).
- **Nontrivial technical work** in proving resilience for greedy methods despite the loss of submodularity/monotonicity under perturbed oracles.
- **Clear theorem statements** that expose how online learning performance depends on offline algorithmic properties (δ and N).


Key weaknesses:

- The reduction is essentially **explore-then-commit**, yielding **T^{2/3}** rates; this is consistent with known barriers in structure-free bandit feedback, but it limits practicality when better rates are possible under additional structure.
- The resilience definition appears **strong/uniform** (it is stated for all subsets), while the online reduction only needs accuracy on the **queried** subsets; this mismatch could confuse readers and should be reconciled more explicitly.
- The algorithm requires (or implicitly uses) knowledge/upper bounds of **δ, N, h** (and horizon **T**) to set exploration length; it is unclear how robust the method is to misspecification or how to tune in practice.
- The paper is heavily theoretical and (as provided) does not include empirical validation; while not required, experiments could materially improve confidence and interpretability of constants and regimes.

**Claims Explanation:**
The central claims are theoretical (definition + reduction + regret/CCV bounds + resilience proofs). 

A formal resilience definition for bi-criteria approximation algorithms and an explanation of why it is the “right” offline property for their online conversion are given.

Problem-specific resilience theorems/corollaries for SC, SCSC, and FSM, including explicit parameter dependencies are provided (proofs in appendix, can be verified with coherency).

The authors have also provided an explicit offline-to-online algorithm description (two-phase exploration/exploitation) together with a proof sketch/derivation of the regret and CCV bounds using concentration (Hoeffding) and the offline resilience guarantee.


Parameter assumptions and techniques to overcome major hurdles when compared to classical proofs are stated. However, assumptions in the online model should be stated more crisply. For e.g., the analysis relies on i.i.d. sampling/concentration for each queried action and bounded rewards/costs; the text suggests stochastic draws with fixed means, but the exact independence/stationarity assumptions (and whether reward and cost are independent) are not explicitly. While not completely necessary as these assumptions are well-known among domain experts, they do increase the rigor the of a theory paper.

**Audience Explanation:**
- The work sits at the intersection of **approximation algorithms**, **online learning/bandits**, and **constrained optimization**, all of which are well represented in TMLR’s readership.
    
- The proposed abstraction (bi-criteria resilience) is a **conceptual contribution** that may be reusable beyond the three worked examples—especially for researchers exploring stability of combinatorial optimization under noisy evaluation and those building oracle-based online learning algorithms.

- The reduction from offline algorithm to online algorithms in the setting of **bandit feedback** for combinatorial actions with competing objectives/constraints is a meaningful attempt that could arouse interests in deepening the techniques and the corresponding proof methodologies.

**Requested Changes:**
1. **Clarify the stochastic model and independence assumptions used in Theorem 3 (and related results).**  
    Concretely: specify whether, for each action $(A)$, (${f_t(A)}_t$) and (${g_t(A)}_t$) are i.i.d. across time with fixed means; whether reward and cost are independent conditional on $(A)$; and whether any adaptive dependence is allowed. This is essential because the proof uses concentration for empirical means.
2. **Reconcile the resilience definition (uniform oracle error for all sets) with what the online reduction actually requires (accuracy only on queried sets).**

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
The submission is primarily methodological/theoretical, no major ethical implications or concerns that would require such statement.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
## **Summary**
This paper examines bi-criteria combinatorial decision making in the bandit setting. At each step, a learner chooses a combinatorial action  and receives only the sum of two values: an objective and a constraint-related metric , both of which are noisy. The learner aims to achieve close to the optimal offline solution for the objective while maintaining a small total constraint violation. The key abstraction is the general concept of resilience for offline bi-criteria approximation algorithms.
An offline bi-criteria approximation algorithm is resilient if it still produces approximately optimal and approximately feasible solutions even if it has slightly imprecise oracle access to the objective and constraint functions. This definition provides a clean interface: once an offline algorithm is shown to be resilient, it can be easily transferred to the online bandit setting.
Based on this insight, this paper provides a black-box offline-to-online transfer. The above reduction implements the offline algorithm by replying to each of its oracle queries with empirical averages computed by repeatedly executing the queried action. After a controlled number of rounds on this exploration step, the learner locks in the set returned by the offline algorithm
for the remaining rounds. The analysis shows that the resulting online procedure achieves sublinear objective regret and sublinear cumulative constraint violation, with rates that depend on (i) the offline algorithm's query complexity and (ii) its resilience parameters. Finally, the framework is instantiated for several important submodular and fairness-constrained problem classes by proving that standard greedy-style offline algorithms satisfy the required resilience conditions. Overall, the paper offers a general and modular path from resilient offline
bi-criteria approximation to online bandit algorithms with provable guarantees.

## **Key Comments**
This paper provides a strong theoretical contribution with a clean and well-motivated message: formalize a robust offline concept of resilience and then leverage it to build an online solution for bi-criteria combinatorial bandits under bandit feedback. The message is clean, and the problem-specific instantiations are believable, and the authors pay close attention to the technical details, including identifying and correcting a commonly repeated but incorrect generalization in the literature. 

The limitations are mostly quantitative and interpretational. On the quantitative side, the results may contain large constants due to the dependence on the offline query complexity $N$  and the resilience parameter $\delta$. On the interpretational side, the paper’s “adversarial” terminology for oracle noise may raise the bar for what the online theory actually assumes, since the reduction ultimately uses bounded i.i.d. stochastic feedback to achieve concentration during exploration.

**Claims Explanation:**
I have briefly reviewed the proofs, and to the best of my understanding, they seem correct.

**Audience Explanation:**
The paper is timely and offers a solid mathematical framework for the problem. I am confident the community will benefit from these results.

**Requested Changes:**
In the paper, “adversarial” mainly refers to worst-case, bounded oracle inaccuracies in the offline resilience definition i.e., the offline algorithm remains approximately correct even if the oracle values are perturbed within a small neighborhood. But the online reduction and regret/CCV guarantees rely on stochastic i.i.d., bounded feedback so that repeated plays yield the desired concentration bound. This, in my opinion is a stochastic bandit assumption, not an adversarial bandit model. So a reader may interpret “adversarial” as meaning adaptive, non-stochastic bandit noise, and expect techniques/guarantees that hold under that stronger setting. That mismatch can cause confusion about what is actually being proved.

N/A

The authors study study bi-criteria combinatorial optimization under noisy function evaluations introducing a new notion of resilience that captures the complexity of the problem. **Requested Changes:**
The paper is clear and properly justified, The scopes are well and explained and also the contributions are stated clearly without overstatements. Many concepts seems genuinely new and well investigated and it seems to me overall a significant theoretical contribution to the literature, I have appreciated how the resilience definition enables an offline-online conversion of the analysis. Since the regret are new there' no state of the art to compare it, but from what I now from similar literature are in line with the lower bounds of similar setting. The notation is clear (and adopts most of the standard from bandit and online learning literature) and the related works are properly discussed. While I understand the focus is mainly theoretical I would have liked to see some experiments, even in the most speculative works on bandits (see some Kaufmann works) some empirical validation is provided. In order to make the exposition cleaner I would suggest to condense the proof of Theorem 3, and leave mainly hints and highlights of the parts of the proof you think may be interesting outside the scope of the work itself. As I said I think the contributions are clear, but it would be even better if the new analysis techniques they've introduced were discussed inthe broader framework of the literature, explaining the progress with respect of previous literature that relies on exact submodularity (in order to better explain myself, is often the case that in bandit learning some new concentration inequality is derived, the authors usually higlhlights this new contribution and explain how can be used outside the scope of the work itself).

There are no broader impact concern

**Additional Comments:**
I think is an excellent paper that provide a theoretical contribution for the field.

The paper tackles an interesting problem. However, the novelty is limited: the proposed method is a straightforward combination of two existing techniques. The writing is also difficult to follow in Sections 3-4, with undefined notation. On the positive side, the experimental evaluation is thorough, covering five datasets with proper ablations.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper proposes to treat graph structure learning from a variational perspective, inspired by previous literature on Gaussian processes, where the connection is that simpler discriminative models encourage sparsity in the learned structure. Regularizing the entropy of the covariance matrix over parameters seems to implicitly induce sparser structures, which is the most relevant contribution of the paper.

**Claims Explanation:**
Mostly (see requested changes).

The authors claim that the regularization bias over sparsity can naturally emerge from a specific variational treatment, which is not necessarily interesting per se. What is interesting is that there is a good correlation between the validation loss and the approximation of the marginal likelihood; in my opinion, this could have been investigated more and reported for additional datasets to provide more conclusive evidence. So, I tend to agree that there is value in modeling the problem this way.

The second main claim is that the performances are improved this way. This is less interesting from a methodological perspective, considering that there are other techniques performing better overall. However, compared to the base versions of the classifiers, which have been properly tuned against different hyper-parameters, there seems to be utility in the approach given close or state of the art results.

**Audience Explanation:**
I think the graph ML audience might want to get more familiar with the reasons why this approximation of the marginal likelihood is a good proxy for validation accuracy, and what are further approximations that may destroy this advantage.

**Requested Changes:**
The paper is generally well written and the appendix has enough details for derivations.

I would like to ask the authors to:
- Better clarify what is the generative model they are computing a variational approximation against
- If possible, provide time/memory cost of training other baselines (in Appendix D.6 one can only see the cost of the authors' approach)
- Better explain, for the reader, the approximation of Equation 8

Right now, the only claim that does not seem supported by evidence is that the variance of the Gumbel-Softmax approximation is higher than a REINFORCE approach. I would like to ask the authors to empirically validate this.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
Nothing to report.

**Additional Comments:**
If the authors will resolve my concerns satisfactorily and without haste, I would be more than happy to lean for acceptance.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
In this paper, the authors introduce a graph learning method based on a variational approach, that is GNN-agnostic. They introduce a likelihood-based objective that they successively simplify using several approximation steps, including a ``Laplace'' approximation that gives the name to their method, and the so-called Gumbel-softmax trick to handle the discrete structure. In practice, the proposed algorithm performs a kind of alternate minimization between the GNN parameters and the graph structure. They report competitive results, bringing vanilla GNNs in-line with state-of-the-art methods.

**Claims Explanation:**
The experiments are convincing, limitations are discussed and ablation studies are performed.

**Audience Explanation:**
This is a generic method for graph learning that applies to any GNN, and is interesting to the graph ML community at large.

**Requested Changes:**
I do have a few questions;
- regarding the method itself, I'm not sure every derivation/approximation steps is well-justified? For instance, the authors propose to approximate the expectation over $A$ with a sampling (eq (7)), then go *back* to an expectation and present the latter as the most innovative step (eq (8)). For the casual reader it seems a bit hard to justify this, among other steps. Can this be better justified?

- every graph learning method that tries to directly learn each edge $a_{ij}$ may suffer from so-called gradient scarcity (e.g., [1]), or overfitting. Is it not the case here? Can this be discussed? Would a more "high-level" parametric method be possible?


[1] Ghanem et al. Gradient Scarcity in Graph Learning with Bilevel Optimization. TMLR 2025

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The authors propose a variational approach to learn graph structure for graph neural network applications. The main idea is that instead of optimizing difficult combinatorial graph structures by imposing structural constraints, put a posterior on the graph structure and related parameters and perform laplace approximation.

**Claims Explanation:**
I find much of the proposed method/experiments/math to be fine and sound, with one notable exception. I highlight this main concern below: 

1. I find the wording of "posterior" and marginal likelihood currently unclear and inaccurate. 

To have a posterior, we need to specify a prior and a likelihood. What is the target "posterior" that we are approximating?

Expression (2) states the variational approximation q(theta, A) = q(theta) q(A) as the factorized approximation of the true joint posterior. 

However, throughout the entire main text of the article, I do not find any likelihood, nor any prior on theta or A.  

So currently, the meaning of the words posterior/marginal likelihood etc are vacuous.  Either avoid this terminology, or make explicitly clear the target posterior. 

Also, in entire subsection 3.2, there is no relation to the data observed D explicitly given. (essential for a posterior interpretation). D appears in expression (5), but that hardly justifies any posterior interpretation since it is simply optimizing an expectation of a loss that depends on the data. 

Currently, the interpretation goes as follows: since the authors are not specifying any priors or likelihoods explicitly, and directly imposing the assumption that the variational approximation of q(theta) is Gaussian and q(A) is bernoulli, the soundness of this assumption is under question. There is little chance that such an approximation is good/justified under any specification of priors/likelihoods. By making the prior/likelihood/posterior explicit, the soundness of the paper can be greatly improved. 

Note: I am not saying the optimization framework couldn't work, I am just saying that the current framing in terms of Bayesian terminology is very confusing and not justified, unless much more information is provided.

**Audience Explanation:**
Graph Learning, GNNs etc are important topics. The approach of using a continuous optimization approach to learn the difficult to learn discrete graph structure is of general interest to audience in this field.

**Requested Changes:**
Please address my concerns in the above section on posterior/Bayesian framing. The resulting revised draft should either be very clear about what the target posterior is and how the current approach is a varational approximation of that, or failing that, avoid the Bayesian terminology/framing. Once this is addressed, I believe the content of the paper would be sufficiently sound for TMLR.

Summary of Contributions

This paper presents a joint verification and refinement framework for improving the safety of large language model (LLM) generated robot programs. The authors propose a method that converts LLM-generated programs into automaton-based representations and verifies them against formal safety specifications using model checking. A key theoretical result, called the compositional verification theorem, proves that any composition of individually verified subprograms will also satisfy safety constraints. This significantly reduces verification complexity for long-horizon tasks.

Building on this, the authors introduce a verification-guided fine-tuning procedure that uses verification outcomes as supervision signals to refine the LLM. Because of the compositional theorem, fine-tuning only needs to cover verified sub-components rather than entire programs, improving both safety compliance and training efficiency.

Empirical evaluations on multiple robot platforms show a 30–50% improvement in the probability of generating safety-compliant programs, about 50% reduction in training time, and good generalization of safety improvements to out-of-domain robots and tasks.

Key Strengths

- Strong theoretical foundation through the compositional verification theorem that provides provable safety guarantees.
- Effective integration of formal verification and LLM fine-tuning to address reliability in safety-critical program generation.
- Demonstrated scalability and transferability across multiple robotic systems.

## Summary

This paper introduces a framework for refining language models to
produce formally safe programs, to improve the efficiency of formally
safe execution of LLM-generated plans in the real world.
Overall, the idea is to prompt an LLM to generate programs using a
given API at train time, run formal verification of these programs
against a given safety specification, and fine-tune (via SFT) the LLM
with the verified safe program outputs. Central to the framework is
the authors' argument that it suffices to verify small "sub-programs"
at train time, which can be safely *composed* to create more complex
and verifiably safe behavior at test-time, drastically reducing the
computation complexity of verification.
After fine-tuning, at deployment, the refined LLM is prompted for
programs until they are verifiably safe, which occurs with much higher
likelihood after the proposed fine-tuning approach in robotic experiments.


## Strengths

I like the idea of fine-tuning an LLM to increase the likelihood of
verifiably-safe program outputs—I think this could be a very
powerful path forward, and may help increase the safety of AI agents
in the real world.
I also think this fine-tuning procedure largely makes sense and sounds
reasonable and inexpensive.
While no confidence intervals are given, the experimental results
appear to be good, demonstrating that the fine-tuning procedure does
significantly reduce the burden of finding safe programs via test-time
search.


## Weaknesses

Unfortunately, the paper suffers from (what are in my opinion) some
major weaknesses, which I discuss one-by-one below (in no particular order).

**Fine-tuning method**.
Overall, the methodology is very difficult to follow. From what it
boils down to (and correct me if I'm wrong), the method is the
following:

1.  Prompt LLM for program
2.  Use formal verification to decide if program is safe according to
    safety specification
3.  Keep only safe programs, fine-tune on them via standard SFT.

This is a fine-tuning approach that is already quite standard in the
literature (e.g., see STaR, cited below). For any fine-tuning task,
these methods do the following:

1.  Prompt LLM for response
2.  Judge response somehow (e.g., is the solution to the math problem correct)
3.  Keep only good responses, fine-tune on them via standard SFT.

So, your method differs only in the sense that the "judge" is a formal
program verifier. I understand that my job as a reviewer for TMLR is
not to assess novelty, and that's fine; my point here is that this
method could have been explained in a much clearer way, while
simultaneously crediting the closely related work. This is especially
true since the construction of the "judge" (i.e., converting source
code into an FSA and validating the FSA) is itself a standard approach
to formal verification. From the perspective of a ML audience, these
details are not as important, and they make it much more difficult to
identify the actual intervention that you did. Moreover, the notation
and equations used to describe the FSAs and such is very confusing,
and in some cases wrong (see below), which only makes matters worse.

**Composition theorem**.
A central focus in the paper is the idea that it suffices to verify
sub-programs to ensure the safety of programs composed of those
sub-programs—this affects the fine-tuning procedure because you then
only need to fine-tune on the generation of much smaller programs.
As I discuss in **Additional Comments**, I am almost certain that this
result is incorrect as stated (Theorem 1), and even if it was corrected, it would
be done at the cost of a *very* strong assumption made on the structure
of the composed programs. Effectively, this assumption would take the
form "if program 1 and program 2 are both safe, then the sequence of
running program 1 followed by program 2 is also safe", at which point,
the proof is trivial (and more importantly, the result is no longer
interesting, because the issue of composition is swallowed by the
assumption). And indeed, if you look at the proof in the
paper, this is basically exactly how it goes.
Similarly, I am also extremely confident that Proposition 2 is
incorrect, and in fact, I believe the incorrectness of Proposition 2
extends even beyond an issue with Theorem 1.

To be clear, I think there are *some* cases of composed programs where
the result holds, but these cases are restricted to ones where the
safety of the composition is obvious *a priori*.

**Experiments**.
As I explain below, the experimental setup in some parts is very
unclear. Most notably, I can't tell if the quantitative results
actually apply to "composed programs"—it seems like they don't. In
fact, the paper doesn't really describe how one *should* execute
composed programs in the proposed framework.

**Claims Explanation:**

for the deployment of composed programs, which was a main motivation for
their work.

**Audience Explanation:**
The problem setup is very relevant, certainly a large part of the TMLR

The paper introduces Highlighted Chain-of-Thought (HoT), a novel inference-time prompting technique. The method instructs a Large Language Model (LLM) to first re-format a given question by wrapping key facts in XML tags (e.g., <fact1>...</fact1>). Subsequently, the LLM generates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) answer that explicitly references these tags, thereby grounding its reasoning steps in the facts provided in the original prompt.

Key Strengths:
* The central idea of using tags for internal fact-grounding may be of interest
* The ablation study (Figure 4) demonstrates that the performance gain from HoT is not solely due to the "Repeated Question" (R-Q) baseline
* The technique can be used to generate a high-quality dataset for fine-tuning smaller models, which can be seen as a way of distilling knowledge/reasoning 

Weaknesses:
* The claim that HoT "outperforms other advanced prompting techniques" like Tree-of-Thought (ToT) and Self-Refine (Table 9), is either misleading or it is not well supported by experimental details. What makes this result very surprising is that ToT or Self Refine are very expensive multi prompt strategies, while HoT is only a single pass (or two pass if counting the first question to add the tags). If this is truly the comparison, it would amount to an extremely surprising result, and the paper must provide substantial detail about the way these baselines are calculated to make sure this is. fair comparison. While the paper provides 70+ pages of example prompts of HoT in main paper and appendix, they provide no detail at all about these baselines, making the judgement about the validity of the baseline and comparisons impossible. Therefore, as of now, one of the papers most important and surprising claims, cannot be objectively judged. 
* The paper's primary claim, that HoT "substantially reduces hallucination" (namely in Figure 1) is based on a methodological flaw and/or a misleading statement. The paper relies on SelfCheckGPT, which the cited paper (Manakul et al., 2023) and the authors' own analysis (Appendix R, Figure 12) confirm is a measure of consistency, not factuality. Note that an LLM can consistently output the same hellucinated/incorrect answer, meaning that the two metrics are at best correlated. The authors even state these are "orthogonal metrics", yet build their main finding on this conflation. In another part the authors write "This is because a model’s reasoning could be highly consistent (measured by SelfCheckGPT) but its final answer does not match the ground-truth for a task" So the model could be consistently outputting a wrong result, but that would be counted as a reduction in hallucination, while in this case it is only making the model more certain about its mistake and thus less calibrated. The fact that HoT is advertised as a way to reduce hallucination yet the key metric used to support is consistency is a major misrepresentation of the results. 
* The paper's stated mechanism for why HoT works is based on the notion that tokens inside fact tags receive more attention, however the paper's own analysis in Appendix D disproves its own hypothesis, finding that the content inside the tags actually receives less attention, and only the tags themselves receive more attention. The authors justify this by saying that the tags tokens might function as summary tokens for the facts inside the tags. The paper also fundamentally misrepresents the findings of Silva et al. (2024), which is used to motivate and substantiate their claims. Silva et al. do not claim that LLMs inherently "tend to pay more attention to... XML tags". Rather, Silva et al. propose a method (GUIDE) that mechanistically *forces* the model to pay attention by "adding a bias to the attention scores"  using their own specific tags (<!->).

**Claims Explanation:**
The paper's most significant claims are not supported by accurate or convincing evidence, as elaborated below. 

-  The claim in Table 9 that HoT "outperforms" methods like Tree-of-Thought (ToT), Self-Refine, and Chain-of-Verification (COVE) is highly surprising and would have required substantial detail to support, but on the contrary the paper provides virtually zero detail about the way baselines are calculated. To elaborate why this is so surprising, HoT is a single-pass method while these baselines are complex, multi-call, iterative, and search-based frameworks that have a very high computational and query cost. The authors provide no implementation details or cost analysis for these baselines (even in the appendix), creating the impression that their single pass approach outperforms these much more demanding approaches. The claim of superiority is therefore unsubstantiated and cannot be judged. 

-  Reducing hallucination is unsupported: This claim is based on a misapplication of the SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023) methodology. As confirmed by the paper' own Appendix R, this tool measures response consistency, not factual correctness. The authors themselves concede that "hallucination reduction and accuracy are related but orthogonal metrics", thereby invalidating their own " What they have shown is that HoT makes models more consistent, which is a different claim than reducing hallucination, which is advertised in abstract and much of the rest of paper, is highly misleading. 

- One of the paper's key motivations—that LLMs "tend to pay more attention to content inside XML tags"—is based on a misreading of Silva et al. (2024). That paper forces this behavior with a special mechanism, it does not observe it as a natural property of XML. The paper's own data in Appendix D finds that fact tokens inside XML tags actually receive "less attention in HoT compared to CoT". The paper's introduction is directly contradicted by its own appendix.

**Audience Explanation:**
Because the claims of the paper are not substantiated and supported, as of now the paper is not of interest to the research community.

**Requested Changes:**
- Authors must provide substantial more detail about the way that baselines are calculated, to the extent that these results can be reproduced independently. Without such amount of detail, simply claiming that their method outperforms much more costly method is not a scientifically substantiated and verifiable result. 
- Authors have made numerous misleading statement about hallucination, while in fact they are making the models more consistent. Consistency means the model may be more consistent about its hallucination. The entire framing thus is misleading to readers.
- Authors have argued quite a few times that paying more attention to facts inside XML tags are the reason model performance improves, but in Appendix D they provide a completely contradictory evidence that those tags receive *less attention*, and offer entirely new explanation, that XML tags act as summary tokens. Then why not framing the paper around summarization instead of paying more attention instead?

Contributions:
1. The paper introduces Highlighted Chain-of-Thought (HoT), a prompting technique designed to reduce hallucinations and improve grounding in Large Language Models (LLMs). Its core contributions include:
2. The HoT Framework: A two-step process where an LLM first reformats a question using XML tags to identify key facts and then generates a reasoning chain that references these tags to ground its answer.
3. Performance Benchmarking: Evaluation across 22 tasks and 5 LLMs (including Gemini 1.5 and Llama 3.1), demonstrating consistent accuracy gains.
4. Human Verification Study: An empirical study with 63 users showing that HoT highlights improve verification speed by approximately 25%.
5. Small Model Optimization: Evidence that fine-tuning small models on HoT-formatted data improves their out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy and reduces attention entropy.

Key Strengths:
1. Broad Empirical Scope: The authors tested the method on a diverse array of tasks, including arithmetic, logical reasoning, and long-context puzzles.
2. Human-Centric Evaluation: Unlike many prompting papers, this work measures the actual impact on human-AI collaboration, specifically verification efficiency.
3. Synergy with Existing Methods: The paper proves that HoT can be combined with other advanced techniques like Self-Consistency and ComplexCoT for additive gains.

Key Weaknesses:
1. Increased Token Latency: HoT requires the model to repeat the question, which increases token consumption and latency, particularly for long-context inputs.
2. Human Annotation Overhead: Creating high-quality, task-specific 8-shot demonstrations is a "costly human effort".
3. The "Over-trust" Risk: The highlights tend to fool users into believing incorrect answers are correct, reducing verification accuracy for wrong LLM responses.

1. Hallucination Reduction: Using both SelfCheckGPT (consistency) and LLM-as-a-judge (span-level), the authors demonstrate that HoT lowers hallucination rates across multiple datasets.

2. Accuracy Gains: Table 3 shows significant improvements in "Reasoning Trap" tasks (+11.38 percentage points on average), while Tables 4-7 detail consistent wins across arithmetic and logical reasoning.

3. Mechanistic Insight: Attention entropy analysis (Table 14) provides a technical explanation for why the method works: HoT-finetuned models focus more intensely on key input facts.

4. Ablation Clarity: Figure 4 effectively breaks down the contribution of each component, showing that repeating the question and adding tags independently contribute to performance.

3. Model Efficiency: The section on fine-tuning small models to emulate the reasoning focus of larger models provides a roadmap for developing more capable, lightweight agents.

2. Token/Cost Analysis: A clear comparison of the token overhead vs. accuracy gain is necessary. Specifically, quantify the average percentage increase in prompt length when using HoT compared to standard CoT.

1. Generalization of Tags: The authors found <fact{i}> worked best. Exploring if semantic tags (e.g., <date>, <math_constraint>) further improve performance would strengthen the methodology.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
The primary concern is misplaced user trust. Because HoT makes responses look more authoritative and "grounded" through highlights, users are less likely to catch errors when the model does hallucinate.

Recommendation: The paper should include a section in the Broader Impact Statement discussing the risks of "hallucination cloaking." This paper targets a concrete systems bottleneck in RLVR for LLMs: rollout generation scales well with batching and parallelism, while policy updates become memory- and communication-bound and often require slowdowns. **Strengths**

2. The max-variance rule is supported by a clean structural result with an efficient algorithm.

Algorithm has theoretical proof. The improvement is significant across different settings.

The findings should interest readers working on RL for LLMs and efficient training systems.

If the authors intend to emphasize the “algorithm-agnostic” framing, the paper should include at least one experiment applying PODS to another RLVR optimizer, such as PPO-style training, or provide a compelling argument backed by evidence that the observed gains are not GRPO-specific.

# Summary of contributions

The paper proposes a novel strategy for down-sampling rollouts to improve training speed and sometimes performance in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) settings for fine-tuning LLMs on math reasoning datasets. The idea is well-motivated and simple -- rollout generation is cheap so it makes sense to over-generate rollouts and downsample the most informative ones -- the proposed max-variance downsampling strategy is intuitive and fast to compute (for downsampling from n to m, just take max m/2 and min m/2 reward elements).

## Strengths

1. The simplicity of the idea and motivation for making the most of a cheaper operation of rollout generation makes this idea well-motivated and easy to adopt
1. The primary results (Fig 3 d,e) show a significant speed-up (time to convergence) using GRPO+PODS vs GRPO alone in fine-tuning wall time for training a 3B as well as 7B Qwen2.5 model
1. The ablation study in Appendix A.3 (Fig 5) shows that max-variance has slightly better test accuracy than random down-sampling on the GSM8K dataset
1. The paper promises to release code upon publication that extends the HuggingFace open-r1 library which will facilitate easy adoption for the community

## Weaknesses

Datasets: The GSM8K and MATH datasets alone are not convincing enough to represent a broad range of available reasoning datasets for fine-tuning LLMs. The results would have been more convincing if the paper had chosen: 
1. Better math reasoning datasets (e.g. improved version of GSM like GSM8k-platinum, GSM1k to control for data contamination/memorization) -- see “Reasoning or Memorization? Unreliable Results of Reinforcement Learning Due to Data Contamination” for an investigation on why Qwen2.5 family of models may have memorized math reasoning benchmarks
2. Reasoning datasets beyond mathematics e.g. in the domain of symbolic logic, strategy, law, medicine, etc

Dataset x model variations: The Llama3.2 model was only evaluated on GSM8K, not MATH -- it would have been informative to know how Llama does despite its weaker performance (especially because of the possibility of Qwen2.5 memorizing GSM8K due to data contamination)

**Claims Explanation:**
Unfortunately the choice of datasets in the paper has led to results that are not convincing of the true potential of the max-variance downsampling idea

**Audience Explanation:**
The findings, even though they are limited by the choice of datasets, warrant publication so as to give justice to the simple and elegant idea of max-variance downsampling which has potential of improving convergence speed in more general settings

**Requested Changes:**
## Suggestions
1. (critical) Add more datasets (as described in earlier) to ensure that the results are not affected by data contamination and are truly generalizable
1. (not critical) The m x n choice ablation experiments (Fig 4) don’t show much benefit for increasing N, this demonstrates that additional rollout samples are not “informative”. Given that the motivation provided in the paper for downsampling is that it is cheap to gather rollouts, this raises a natural next question about: How can rollouts be generated in a smarter manner? There are several ideas that come to mind: 
    * Instead of max-variance, how about first breaking the reward range into equal sized bins and picking equal number of samples from each? -> this would downsample the over-represented reward values and lead to more informative updates, in line with the motivation presented in the paper
    * The “reward distribution” is not taken into account -- if we can bias the model to intentionally produces samples with a specified reward, we can “hack” the rollout generation procedure to only produce samples near the “max” and “min” end of reward, this would be something similar to the “Decision Transformer” paper (2021) where the model is conditioned on the desired reward
1. (not critical) The appendix section A.3 seems more important than the proof for max-variance downsampling being computable with a simple sort and taking m/2 top and bottom elements, I would recommend swapping the position of these sections.

This work propose BN-Pool, the first soft-clustering pooling operator capable of adaptively determining the number of supernodes for each individual graph. Unlike previous methods that rigidly fix # of supernodes or set it as a fraction of graph size, BN-Pool utilizes a Bayesian Non-parametric framework with a Dirichlet Process prior to allow for a theoretically unbounded number of clusters. This is implemented via a variational autoencoder where a GNN approximates the posterior of node-to-cluster assignments, optimized by combining downstream task loss with an auxiliary reconstruction loss.

In node clustering tasks, e.g., community detection, this work effectively identifies communities and interaction patterns without prior knowledge of the number of classes, reconstructing adjacency matrices that better reflect the original graph sparsity compared to methods like MinCut. 

In graph classification, the method performs on par with or superior to existing pooling operators, achieving state-of-the-art results on datasets such as Colors-3 and Enzymes. BN-Pool avoids the redundancy typical of other soft-clustering methods by generating compact pooled graphs that preserve informative content while discarding unnecessary clusters.

**Claims Explanation:**
Theoretically,  the core evidence for the model's ability to adaptively determine the # of nodes comes from the properties of DP, which dictates that even with infinite capacity, the process will favor reusing existing components, and using the Stick-Breaking Process to construct the mixing proportions.

Additionally, this work demonstrates effectiveness from multiple experimental perspectives, e.g., adaptive clutering ability, competitive performance and compact representations.

**Audience Explanation:**
This article is based on the classic DP scheme for graph clustering. This simple combination of traditional schemes with neural networks should be of interest to the audience.

**Requested Changes:**
The experimental validation would benefit from a more rigorous analysis of the model's robustness and the specific contributions of its components. Specifically, the paper lacks a sensitivity analysis for the hyperparameter $\eta$ in Equation 12, which balances the reconstruction loss and clustering penalty; it is crucial to demonstrate whether extreme values of $\eta$ cause the model to degenerate into trivial solutions, such as assigning all nodes to a single cluster. Furthermore, since BN-Pool introduces three distinct loss terms, an explicit ablation study is necessary to quantify the independent performance contribution of each term. Finally, while the paper highlights successful clustering on datasets like GCB-H, the discussion should be expanded to include failure cases or specific scenarios where the model struggles, such as on heterophilic graphs, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of its limitations.

Regarding complexity and scalability, the reliance on an $O(N^2)$ reconstruction loss poses a clear challenge for scaling to larger graphs, despite the authors' assertion that it is manageable for current benchmarks. The paper should discuss or propose specific optimization strategies to mitigate this, such as employing edge sampling or negative sampling to approximate the loss and potentially reduce complexity to $O(|E|)$ or $O(N)$. Additionally, the current runtime comparison relies solely on time-per-epoch, which may be misleading; given the complex variational inference and auxiliary losses involved, BN-Pool likely requires more epochs to converge than simpler baselines. Therefore, comparing the total time required to reach convergence would offer a more realistic and transparent assessment of the training costs.

This paper studies how concepts are represented jointly in large language models (LLMs). The main contribution is a geometric framework based on Concept Realization Manifolds (CRMs), which treats a concept as a region of activation space rather than as a single direction. Building on this view, the paper introduces Multi-Concept Activation Subspaces (MCAS) to analyze multiple concepts together, distinguishes directional entanglement from measure entanglement, proposes conditional disentanglement via orthogonal projection, and evaluates concept-aligned interventions for bias mitigation and spillover control.

**Strengths**: the paper tackles an important and timely question; the distinction between directional alignment and activation-distribution overlap is conceptually useful; and the paper tries to connect interpretability, bias analysis, and intervention within a unified framework.

**Weaknesses**: the strongest theoretical claims are not fully matched by the empirical evidence; some evaluation choices require stronger justification, especially the use of CAV-based proxy metrics; and several empirical results, including baseline behavior and uncertainty reporting, need clearer explanation.

**Claims Explanation:**
I am not yet convinced that the current evidence fully supports the paper’s strongest claims.

My main concern is the gap between the theoretical framing and the empirical validation. The paper’s central theoretical message is that, under correlated concepts and prediction-preserving representations, measure entanglement may remain even when concept directions are orthogonalized. However, the experiments do not directly verify the key assumptions behind this claim, such as the relevant concept dependence structure or the prediction-preserving impossibility result. In practice, the experiments mostly show that orthogonalization does not eliminate observed overlap, which is suggestive but not equivalent to validating the stronger theorem-level conclusion.

I also found the empirical validation of “independence” between directional entanglement and measure entanglement unconvincing as currently presented. One quantity is effectively fixed for a concept pair while the other varies with thresholding, so interpreting the resulting undefined or degenerate correlation behavior as confirmation of independence is too strong.

A second concern is metric validity. Several reported quantities, including LMS, SS, and ICAT, are computed using CAV-based proxy probabilities rather than the language model’s actual output probabilities. This is a consequential methodological choice, but the paper does not provide enough validation to show that these proxy metrics support the same interpretation as the standard metrics.

Finally, some intervention tables are difficult to interpret. In multiple tables, the TCAV and Independent baselines appear numerically identical across models, and many reported uncertainties are exactly or nearly zero despite multiple seeds and bootstrap intervals. These patterns need explanation, because they currently weaken confidence in the empirical comparison.

**Audience Explanation:**
Yes. I expect at least part of the TMLR audience would be interested in this paper because it addresses a relevant problem at the intersection of representation analysis, concept-based interpretability, and bias evaluation in large language models. In particular, the paper asks a useful question: when multiple concepts are jointly represented, is concept interference best understood as directional alignment, activation overlap, or both? That question is timely and potentially valuable even though I do not find the current evidence fully convincing.

**Requested Changes:**
The paper’s main theorem is stronger than what the current experiments establish. Right now, the empirical section shows that overlap can remain after orthogonalization in the studied settings, but it does not directly validate the theorem’s stronger prediction-preserving impossibility claim. Please either test the theorem’s assumptions and implications more directly, or narrow the claim to match the evidence.

The “independence” validation between directional entanglement and measure entanglement should also be redesigned. As currently written, one quantity is effectively fixed for a concept pair while the other varies with thresholding, so the analysis does not amount to a convincing demonstration of statistical independence.

The LMS/SS/ICAT evaluation needs stronger justification. These quantities are computed from CAV-derived proxy probabilities rather than the model’s actual output probabilities, which materially changes how the results should be interpreted. Please either validate the proxy scores against the standard metrics or present them explicitly as proxy measures and narrow the claims accordingly.

The paper should explain why TCAV and the Independent baseline are numerically identical across several key tables. If these are genuinely different methods, the implementation difference should be stated clearly, together with an explanation of why the evaluation fails to separate them.

The uncertainty estimation procedure also needs clarification. Given five seeds and bootstrap intervals, the large number of exactly or nearly zero error bars is surprising. Please specify what is resampled, what randomness remains across runs, and why the reported variance is so small.

The paper would also benefit from one or two worked examples that follow a concrete input through concept scores, overlap, and intervention. The current presentation has useful schematic intuition, but it lacks enough concrete case studies.

It would also help to simplify the terminology and focus the presentation on the few objects that are actually carrying the paper’s argument. At present, the number of introduced terms feels larger than necessary.

Finally, releasing code, annotations, and enough implementation detail would make the empirical claims easier to independently check.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
Because the paper studies interventions on socially meaningful concepts such as bias- and safety-related attributes, I think a Broader Impact Statement would be appropriate if one is not already included. In particular, the paper should discuss the risk of misuse of activation-space interventions on sensitive attributes, the normative assumptions behind labeling concepts such as bias or harmfulness, and the possibility that reducing one problematic dimension can worsen another through spillover.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper argues that concept representations in neural activations should be analyzed beyond single Concept Activation Vectors, especially when multiple socially meaningful or safety-relevant concepts are correlated.
It proposes a probe-dependent geometric framework in which a concept is represented by a probe-defined activation region, introduces a distinction between "directional entanglement" and "overlap-based entanglement", and claims that the latter can persist even after directional orthogonalization.
Building on this view, the paper proposes a multi-concept activation subspace method for more targeted interventions and reduced spillover across concepts.

**Claims Explanation:**
The paper does provide some support for its main intuition that concept entanglement is not exhausted by angular alignment of concept directions, and it offers experiments consistent with the idea that overlap-based entanglement can persist even after orthogonalization.
It also reports some empirical results for conditional disentanglement, so the submission is not purely speculative.

However, several central claims are not supported in a fully convincing or clear way.
The theoretical claims are also weaker than the presentation suggests.
More broadly, the paper's evidence is often obscured by imprecise terminology.
Several proposed constructs are not mathematically well specified enough to support the theoretical weight placed on them, which makes the argument harder to assess and reduces confidence in the claimed novelty.

Take the so-called "Concept Entanglement Field" as an example, which is arguably an important terminology mentioned in the abstract.
The author says it is a "structured overlap regions where concepts are entangled."
The Definition A.5 "more formally" defines it is a "structured overlap region such that no local tangent isolates one concept without sensitivity to the other."

This has several problems.
First, "structured" is empty unless the structure is specified.
Topological? Differential? Statistical? Algebraic?
If nothing is stated, then "structured" is decorative language, not mathematics.
Second, "region" is also vague.
Calling it a "field" adds no content.
It is not a vector field, tensor field, or anything field-like in the mathematical sense.
Third, the notion of "no local tangent isolates one concept without sensitivity to the other" is not formalized well enough.
What does "isolates" mean?
The definition gestures at a phenomenon, but does not pin it down.
So the term gives you the illusion of having identified a new object, while in fact you still do not know what the object is.

A good mathematical definition should identify a genuinely new object or isolate a property that matters, so we can make statements easier to formulate and prove, or reveal structure that was previously obscured.
This term, along with other proposed terms like Conditional Concept Manifolds, Intersectional Concept Regions, etc., do none of that.
Calling the defined things "manifolds" is especially annoying, because nothing in the formalism really uses manifold structure in a meaningful way.
This matters because bad terminology does real damage.
It makes the reader spend effort learning names instead of ideas, and it hides which parts are mathematically substantive and which are not.

The paper has one potentially worthwhile intuition: whether two concepts are “disentangled” should depend on what a probe can actually read out, not on some intrinsic geometry of the representation.
But then the paper undermines its own good intuition by dressing it up using math-flavored prestige vocabulary without building the actual mathematical infrastructure that would justify those words.

Overall, I would say the paper contains suggestive evidence for an interesting intuition, but the strongest claims are oversold relative to the clarity and rigor of the supporting evidence.

**Audience Explanation:**
The paper addresses a topic that many TMLR readers care about: how to reason about concept representations, disentanglement, and intervention in modern neural models, especially for socially meaningful or safety-relevant attributes.
Its central intuition, that entanglement should be understood in a probe-dependent and multi-concept way rather than purely through single concept directions, is relevant to researchers in interpretability, representation learning, fairness, and safety.

**Requested Changes:**
Please provide clean and rigorous definitions and reduce terminology inflation.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The application of fine-tuning LLMs with federated learning is important. The authors provide a more efficient zeroth-order solution that improves accuracy and convergence compared with existing zeroth-order methods for fine-tuning.

### Strengths
1. The proposed method improves accuracy, convergence, and efficiency, supported by both empirical results and theoretical analysis.
2. The evaluation demonstrates improvements over existing zeroth-order methods.

### Weaknesses
1. Since the authors compare with the baseline FedAvg (LoRA), they may also want to demonstrate that the proposed solution works with LoRA as well.
2. It is somewhat unfair to compare only with SGD as the baseline, since zeroth-order methods are mainly based on gradient estimation. For FedAvg (LoRA), users can also employ other optimizers such as Adam, AdamW, or clipping techniques to significantly improve convergence.
3. The authors should also consider quantization. To reduce memory usage, quantization is commonly introduced during training. The authors may need to demonstrate that the proposed zeroth-order method can work well with quantized models.

### Minor Comments
1. The two algorithms are somewhat difficult to read, especially due to the large number of notations and terminologies. The authors may consider organizing them more clearly. For example, the right side of Figure 1 does not provide much useful information, and the authors may consider improving Figure 1.
2. The authors may also consider evaluating the method on larger models.

**Claims Explanation:**
I think most of the claims are supported by evidence, but there are still some claims that are not completely supported, as listed in the Weakness section.

I also have several questions that the authors may want to discuss or clarify.

1. I am wondering whether the proposed method can be applied to LoRA fine-tuning and other LoRA-based extensions. In particular, the method requires blocks for perturbation. For LoRA matrices, would such perturbations still be appropriate given the different magnitudes typically observed in LoRA parameters?

2. How does the choice of the split position $l$ affect the performance?

3. It would also be beneficial to compare with other optimizers such as AdamW. One drawback of AdamW is its higher memory consumption due to storing additional optimizer states. Since the proposed method aims to reduce memory usage, demonstrating comparable performance to FedAvg (LoRA) with AdamW would make the method particularly compelling.

**Audience Explanation:**
Large language model training, federated learning, and zeroth-order fine-tuning are cutting edge topics and of certain importance to resolve.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
This paper proposes FedSPZO, a zeroth-order federated learning method that splits the model into two blocks, aiming to balance between computation, memory and communication efficiency. While the idea of leveraging model structure for more efficient ZO gradient estimation is interesting, the paper suffers from fundamental issues in practice and algorithmic presentation.

**Claims Explanation:**
The core claims are supported by experimental results. The experimental results provided in the paper are good, but I have additional concerns regarding the practical use cases of the proposed algorithm. The algorithm description can be improved.

**Audience Explanation:**
The paper would interest members of the TMLR audience working on federated learning and LLM fine-tuning.

**Requested Changes:**
* I think the proposed method has significant limitations, as it is hard to generalize to generation tasks. Currently, all experiments evaluate only classification tasks. One major concern is that for generative models, the last linear layer is the language modeling head with vocabulary projection. This makes the overhead of the proposed method no longer negligible, and the entire efficiency benefit collapses. Thus, performance on complex tasks like instruction following, dialogue, and reasoning remains a fundamental limitation.

* The authors mentioned that the proposed FedSPZO achieves a better trade-off between memory, communication, and computation overhead. I think this is not clear, as the "better trade-off" is vague. In my view, loading a LLaMA-3.2-3B alone requires ~6GB of memory, and the memory gap between FedSPZO and LoRA-based fine-tuning is only ~3GB; the difference in communication is not that significant as well. However, FedSPZO requires 17×higher total computation than FedAvg(LoRA) and sometimes suffers from performance drops.

* The algorithm description is not very well organized and is quite hard to follow. It is unclear from the pseudocode whether $sl_2$ serves as an input, an output, or both.

* The paper has issues with citation formatting throughout. The authors frequently misuse \citet and \citep, placing citations (including author names and years) directly between a concept and its predicate.
